A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KOCO-BENCH research. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material across appendix renumbering and layout changes.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of LLMs, specialization methods, and coding agents, alongside continual-learning experiments, contamination measurements, and project-generation analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds baseline comparisons, a sequence-length ablation, sampling results, and agent-control experiments in Appendices D-G.

M1.justification: The proposed benchmark construction, knowledge-corpus organization, task formulation, and requirement/test creation procedures remain unchanged in Section 3. Dense RAG and instruction tuning are added comparison baselines, not revisions to the proposed benchmark method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same six domains, eleven frameworks, twenty-five projects, code-generation tasks, and knowledge-understanding questions (Tables 1 and 7). The added experiments reuse this coverage; revised code-length statistics do not establish a dataset change.

E2.justification: Appendix D adds two variants within existing specialization families: Dense RAG using EmbeddingGemma and instruction tuning on Gemini-3-Flash-generated requirement/code pairs (Table 9). The original LLM, agent, and specialization comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds substantial experimental controls: SFT sequence lengths of 4096 and 8192 alongside 2048, and Claude-Sonnet-4-5 as the shared backbone for agent comparisons (Appendices E and G). Appendix D also introduces instruction-supervised training. These supplement the retained original settings; ten-sample Pass@any at temperature 0.8 was already specified in v1.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether short training sequences explain weak SFT performance and whether different base models explain agent performance gaps (Appendices E and G). Appendix F also supplies evidence about success across multiple generation attempts. Existing forgetting, corpus-size, error, contamination, and case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix G.1 already specifies ten samples for Pass@any, retained in v2 Appendix K.1. The new sampling tables do not introduce seed sweeps, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 9-13 add baseline, ablation, sampling, and agent-control results. For example, Claude-backed SWE-Agent and OpenHands achieve 18.5% and 17.5% average Pass@1; these are new configurations, not same-setting improvements over v1. Original main result tables remain unchanged. Section 4.1 corrects 28.2% to 30.3%, matching Table 4; Table 1 revises maximum corpus/project lengths from 40.0k/67.4k to 400.5k/674.0k lines.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces a theoretical contribution. Existing task and metric definitions remain unchanged, including Pass@any already described in v1 Appendix G.1; the new sequence-length conclusions are empirical.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings, and conclusion retain the benchmark's novelty and scope, weak domain performance, limited specialization gains, forgetting findings, and Claude Code's 34.2% result. Additional supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly recognizes the agent-backbone confound and interprets the controlled results as showing a remaining agent-system gap. It also interprets tested sequence lengths as having limited influence on SFT performance and discusses multi-attempt performance ceilings. The original limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix K.2 newly documents random file concatenation, endoftext separators, fixed-length training chunks, and use of all chunks for SFT/LoRA. Section 4.1 clarifies agents' project/corpus access, and Appendix D identifies the new retriever and training-pair generator. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original implementations.

R1.justification: V2 removes the RiskAtlas citation and reference. Research positioning otherwise remains stable. Duplicate Yu and Zheng bibliography entries are consolidated without removing the underlying cited works.

P1.justification: V2 makes limited prose additions around agent controls and implementation details, inserts Appendix sections D-G, and updates cross-references, author information, and funding acknowledgments. The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained.

P2.justification: Five new tables present baseline variants, sequence-length ablations, paired Pass@1/Pass@any results, and agent controls, substantially extending the appendix's tabular presentation. The existing contamination table becomes Table 14. Table 2 is enlarged/reformatted, Figure 2 moves, Figure 3 is resized, and other retained material reflows.

improvement.justification: V1's agent comparison mixes base models; v2 Table 13 controls that important confound and strengthens interpretation of agent differences. Additional retrieval/training baselines and sequence-length tests address plausible explanations for weak specialization performance. Corpus-packing documentation and corrected numerical summaries improve reproducibility and consistency. Together these substantially strengthen the empirical support for the paper, although equal inference budgets are not established for the new agent controls.
